en: Of him whose family name was [bestowed] for his protection of the herds of cows terrified by the onset of the irresistible force of the clouds,
and who treated the circle of the earth with easeful pride.
May the lifting of Govardhana by Murāri be for our delight.

This work, with its slightly deep-seated joints, serves as the cause for the manifestation of that Prakrit which is characterized by various contortions and regional peculiarities, and which now terrifies those of dull intellect.
A composition that turns artificial deception into ink.
I bow to those misers and wicked men who, while claiming to be wise, declare that even a correspondence of synonymous words constitutes theft.
Bhavabhūti was a poet whose collection of virtues was sung by the world;
this composition of his is the work titled *Mālatīmādhava*.

[1] (1) Now, following the tradition of the sages such as Bharata, who maintain that the *nāndī*—consisting of twelve or eight *padas* and marked by the word "moon" (*candra*)—should contain a benediction at its beginning regarding the dramatic form (*rūpaka*) and so forth, the author accepts the position of the eight-*pada* variety. Since the word *pada* has two meanings—referring either to a syllable ending in a case-suffix (*vibhaktyanta-varṇa*) or to a quarter-verse (*ślokaturīyāṃśa*)—he adopts the first mode with the initial verse, and then, intending to include the second mode, he introduces another verse beginning with "api ca," saying: "Cūḍāpīḍa... [C2].

(2) *Cūḍāyām*: on the crest, that is, on the topknot (*śikhā*); the *āpīḍa* is a garland bound crosswise. [The phrase means: those [streams] in which the water of the Mandākinī flows down, pervaded by the skull-bowls belonging to that [garland]. Here, by implication, the "garland" consists of the skull-bowls themselves. And because they are pervaded by skull-bowls, the water also trickles down after having slipped over them. The *bhujaṅga*s themselves are the *vallī*s: the creepers; these very [creepers], situated in the form of coils (*valaya*)—that is, in a circular shape—are the *sraj*s: flower-garlands; by these, the *jūṭa* (topknot) is *naddha*: bound.

And here, by one who perceives that the entire portion of the eye contained within the eyelid is composed of light, it is said: "the eyelid of the forehead-eye" [B1b]. To think that there is impropriety in the statement, "What is this suspicion of a *ketaka* flower-tuft upon the head of the Lord of Beings (*Bhūteśa*)? belongs only to one devoid of intelligence, since impropriety itself is the cause of doubt. (3) And here, regarding the mass of matted hair (*jaṭājūṭa*), by its very nature...

By means of the serpent-coil, which is intensely dark, he displays the rising of clouds; by the dripping of the waters of the Mandākinī, the rain; by the garland of skulls, the row of cranes; by the light of the eye on his forehead, the flash of lightning; and by the crescent moon, which resembles the delicate tip of a ketaka bud, he displays the appearance of tender ketakīs. Thus, by indicating the season of the clouds—the primary cause for the agitation of the god of love—he demonstrates that the essence of this dramatic work is the erotic sentiment (*śṛṅgārarasa*).

Although even the spring season does not forfeit its status as a repository of the magnificent excitants (*uddīpana-vibhāva*) for the erotic sentiment (*śṛṅgāra*), nevertheless, the prioritization of the rainy season is intended to indicate the fulfillment of the pacification of boundless torment. [1]

[2] Now, indicating that this composition is worthy of being enacted on stage and ensuring the accomplishment of all desired goals without obstacle, he speaks joyfully, presenting an *nāndī* of eight words—consisting of four quarters of a verse—as follows: "With joy... Here too, the snakes' pursuit of their holes out of fear of peacocks delighted by the deep, resonant roar is a sign of the rainy season.

And thus it is indicated that this narrative, which constitutes the subject matter of the present work (*prakaraṇa*), has now reached its commencement with the onset of the rainy season. As he will say later: "Now these days have arrived, fragrant from the earth being drenched by showers, carrying the splendor of the transition between the departure of the summer heat and the arrival of the rains. (4) Furthermore, in this context, "enjoyment" (*bhoga*) refers specifically to the body of the Lord of Serpents (*phaṇipati*). And for those seeking an opening...

The contraction of the bodies of serpents is their natural birthright; the *tāṇḍava* dance of the Trident-bearer is the description of the moment of slaying Nandin and Muraja. And here, by striking Muraja, instrumental music (*vādya*) is provided; by making the quarters resound with his garland of bees, song (*gīta*) is provided; and by the shaking of his face, dance (*nṛtya*) is indicated—thus the triple symphony (*tauryatrika*) is displayed. Furthermore, by his roar (*cītkāra*), the clearly manifest recitation (*pāṭha*) of one who dances is suggested. [2]

"Sūtradhāra" [is the stage direction]. The ellipsis is "having entered, he speaks. The exclamation "Aye! indicates agitation because, being intent on performing the necessary morning rites, the rising of the sun had not yet been perceived, and one suddenly beholds its light. "Bhūyiṣṭham" means "much. "Much of this blessed one's portion has risen; only a very little remains for his rising"—this is the meaning. Therefore, "I shall worship him," that is to say, [the Sun]. The meaning is: "By means of a verse composed by myself, which sets forth the Supreme Deity, I shall manifest my reverence toward him as if he were a sacred mantra."

[3] You alone, O Great One, rule over auspicious things here in this world. "Auspicious things" (*kalyāṇāni*) means desired blessings; of these, you alone, O Great One—meaning you who are beyond even the reach of the minds of others—rule supremely here in this world. The meaning is that you have the power to bestow them upon your devotees, for the Blessed One is renowned as the wish-fulfilling tree (*kalpavṛkṣa*) that brings about the fulfillment of the vast and expansive prayers of the hearts of all people, just like the sun itself. You ordain the meritorious...

"Lakṣmīm" means: you especially bear (*dhatse*) auspicious (*puṇyām*), that is, beautiful (*manojñām*), fortune (*lakṣmīm*), meaning splendor (*śobhām*); or, you bring about a lovely prosperity. "Atha" is used as a conjunction (*samuccaye*), as they say: "The word *atha* is used in the senses of inquiry, commencement, sequence, promise, and conjunction. (5) "Bestow your glance upon me"—the meaning is, "look at me. However, in the reading "you are the lord of great blessings" (*kalyāṇānāṃ tvam asi mahatām īśiṣe*), "you are" (*asi*) means "you become. "To give" (*dātum*) is as before. "Of the great" (*mahatām*): [refers to those who possess great virtues].

"Among the radiant ones, you prevail; you exist with preeminence. In the reading "O Viśvamūrti, you are the vessel of auspicious splendors," however, "splendors" (*mahaḥ*) refers to radiances, and "auspicious" (*kalyāṇānām*) refers to those whose nature is auspicious; you are their substratum. (6) By the repetition "whatever... whatever" (*yad yad*), there is an indication of the threefold sins of speech, mind, and body. "Repel" (*pratijahi*): repel that sin which afflicts us; repel it in its opposite direction. The word "that" (*tat*) contains an implicit repetition.

The meaning of "tat tat" is "that and that. "Bhadraṃ bhadram" means "auspicious, auspicious"—that is, grant me what is excellent and desirable, free from defect. "Maṅgalam" refers to a form worthy of being aspired for; [this is requested] for that which is most abundant. Furthermore, here, the commencement of the morning worship of the Lord Bhānu (the Sun), bypassing deities such as Hari, Hara, and Hiraṇyagarbha, is appropriate because the protagonist of the work to be undertaken is a Brāhmaṇa. For this very reason, the request "grant [me]" is a supplication befitting a Brāhmaṇa.

If it is argued that it is appropriate to attend upon the Sun (the progenitor of the night) while adorned with ornaments, we say no; for the intention is to express that the time of dawn, being the cause of the destruction of all base creatures, is worthy of respect, since its intended result is the indication of the destruction of wicked beings such as Aghoraghaṇṭa. Having thus praised the Lord Pūṣan, the hero’s request for his desired object is made: "Bestow your glance upon me."

If it is asked, "What is the use of praying for that which results in undesirable fruits from the gaze of malevolent planets?"—the answer is no, because [the Lord] becomes gracious and gentle toward one who has attained devotion. For this very reason, it is said, "Be gracious. Otherwise, the performance of rituals such as sacrifices to the planets would be untenable. By the repetition "whatever... whatever," there is an indication of the crushing of even formidable beings like Śārdūla and Aghoraghaṇṭa.

Immediately after the warding off of evil, through the desire for auspiciousness, the fulfillment of his own wish by the attainment of Mālatī and the fulfillment of his dear friend Makaranda’s wish by the attainment of Madayantikā is indicated; this [fulfillment] is followed by the accomplishment of other desired ends. If he were to desist upon merely attaining those [two], his inability to endure that [separation] would lead him to enter the perilous situation of leaping over the threshold [to commit suicide], whereby the fulfillment of his goal would be tantamount to its non-attainment; therefore, the prayer for deliverance from that state is for the sake of auspiciousness.

By the word "furthermore" (*bhūyaḥ*), the recovery of Mālatī who had been abducted by Kapālakuṇḍalā is indicated, as well as the acquisition of the magic spell (*vidyā*), which he will say: "I extend this incantation (*ākṣepaṇī*) for your welfare. Likewise, it is signaled that there shall be the destruction of all calamities befalling the world connected to Mālatī and Mādhava, by warding off the attempt of Bhūrivasu, Kāmandakī, Madayantikā, Avalokitā, Buddharakṣitā, and Lavaṅgikā—who have their minds tormented by the apprehension of Mālatī’s death—to abandon their lives. (7) [3]

One who is venerable (*mānya*) should be addressed as *bhāva*, while one who is slightly inferior is called *māriṣa*; thus, according to this statement, the address *mārṣa* is used for the purpose of manifesting [the actor’s] status as a subordinate attendant. (8) Because he endures everything when being directed by the *sūtradhāra* and carries out what has been said, he is a *marṣa* (one who endures); hence he is a *mārṣa*. The reading *māriṣa* in the archaic texts is for the purpose of completing the meter. For the pacification of all obstacles, the auspicious rites performed on the stage—such as the worship of the world-protectors (*lokapāla*), which result in the successful completion of the performance—are [performed] excellently.

"According to the prescribed rule" (*vidhānataḥ*): they were ordained. "Assembled" (*saṃnipatitaḥ*): having come from all sides, they gathered together in one place. The phrase "in connection with the festival procession" (*yātrāprasaṅgena*) indicates the occasion for the dance, as it was said: "This glorious festival of the banner of Mahendra is proceeding. (9) "The great people" (*mahājanāḥ*): those who are impartial and possess refined intellects; their "assembly" (*samājaḥ*): their gathering. They are called "Bharatas" because they study the treatise proclaimed by Bharata.

[Pāriplavika: The meaning is that he causes the members of the assembly to cultivate the aesthetic flavors (*rasa*) arising from the nature of the mind. (10) *Pariṣannirdiṣṭaguṇaḥ* means one whose qualities have been pointed out by the assembly.

[Sūtradhāra: The *āryas* are those who have gone far away, having departed from the fruitless, tasteless essence of village life; they are the wise (*vidagdha*). Their minds consist of a cultivation (*bhāvanā*) made beautiful by the flow of well-known narratives capable of instantly grasping reflections, and whose sole life is poetry that produces extraordinary wonder (*alaukika-camatkāra*). The *miśras* are the venerable ones (*pūjya*). (11) The word *miśra* denotes venerability and is always used in the plural; this is seen in the *Viṣṇupurāṇa*: "by Dakṣa together with the *Miśras*, the Marīcis" (*marīcimīśrair dakṣeṇa*). (12) The *bhūmidevas* are the Brahmins.

[NA™Aḥ] [4] "In abundance" means for the most part; "of the sentiments" (rasānām) refers to all ten—namely, the erotic, the comic, the pathetic, the furious, the heroic, the terrible, the odious, the marvelous, the tender, and the peaceful; "applications" (prayogāḥ) refers to compositions beautiful in their structural arrangement; "profound" (gahanāḥ) means they cannot be fully comprehended merely by knowing the rules of grammar and lexicography, but are perceivable only by a select few whose mental power has crossed the ocean of the entire essence of poetry.

(13) By this, it is stated that the literary work (*prabandha*) consists of aesthetic flavor (*rasa*). However, the presence of even a trace of *rasa* establishes the status of a work as a semblance of a literary composition (*prabandhābhāsa*), as is the case with works such as the *Anargharāghava*. Regarding the phrase "delightful through friendship," this is because a work that does not possess such qualities has a core of insipidity and is therefore a semblance of a literary composition, like the *Mudrārākṣasa* and similar works.

(XX) [Objection: But surely, even here there are no actions that are heartwarming through friendship in every respect, because of the contrary nature of the feelings of Kapālakuṇḍalā and Aghoraghaṇṭa toward Mālatī and Mādhava, and likewise those of Kāmandakī toward Nandana; for in some way, there is indeed a heartwarming quality of friendship there as well, due to the existence of a very firm friendship between Cāṇakya and Candragupta. [Reply: No, for by the word "friendship" (*sauhārda*) here, what is intended is partiality that is without a specific motive.

Because it is intended to denote the meaning of the word *sneha* (affection), whereas for Kauṭilya and Vṛṣala, their activities are characterized by a devotion to their respective duties (*kāryopabandha*), such a state [of affection] does not exist. Furthermore, even if friendship (*sauhārda*) were present, there would be no corresponding actions, because of their harsh, cruel, and uneven nature, as evidenced by acts such as the prohibition of the *Kaumudī* festival. *Auddhatya* (arrogance) is the manifestation of contempt for others while placing one's own excellence foremost. Likewise, he has applied the *Kāmasūtra*. Here, "desire" (*kāma*) refers to the longing directed toward an object with beautiful eyes.

That very thing is the *sūtra*: the thread that initiates the weaving of the cloth of communal enjoyment (*saṃbhoga*). Its "ā" is the bringing [of the thread] toward the effect by way of its pervasive presence (*samantādbhāva*); this is the "joining" (*yojana*), for which loftiness (*uddhatatā*) is necessary.

(14) This is what is meant: in this fifth act, the hero’s arrogance does not bring about a failure to embrace the multitude of the hero’s virtues. For, by restoring Mālatī’s life, his passion for her was fully nourished; and as he watched Mālatī—who was being led away toward Nandana—his heart having been stolen by her, his lack of other recourse made his behavior merely assumed (*āhārya*), and thus it is not a fault. However, innate arrogance leads to a fault, as in the case of Rāvaṇa, Paraśurāma, and others. (15) Citrā:

This is the cause for wonder. By this, it is shown that because of the beauty of the subject matter (*kathāvastu*) and other qualities, this work is not at all useless even to the learned; thus, the universal utility of this treatise is demonstrated. As they say: "Poetry leads to fame, to wealth, to knowledge of worldly conduct, to the warding off of misfortune, to immediate supreme bliss, and—by being like a beloved woman—to instruction. (Kāvyālaṅkāra 1.2) [4] *Vidagdhatā* (refinement): maturity, faultlessness, and ingenuity (*vakratva*).

[Sūtradhāra: By the mention of "the Deccan" (*dakṣiṇāpatha*), the author indicates his own proficiency in describing that region because it generates the sentiments of love (*śṛṅgāra*) and heroism (*vīra*). By saying "in Vidarbha," the poet illuminates his own mastery in the acquaintance with the Vaidarbha style. [The verse continues: "Even poets who have traveled long distances follow the style of that land, which possesses the *kaiśikī* mode of expression and whose words exude fragrance. Since he resides in that very land, the adherence to its style is indeed easy for him.

(17) Regarding the phrase "named Padmanagara," the word *nāma* here signifies renown—as in "the Himalaya [is] named [so]"—and does not mean "designation. For if it were used as a modifier (*prakṛtyādi*), there would be the contingency of using the third case, resulting in *Padmanagareṇa nāmnā*; or, if it were a compound, it would have to be *Padmanagaranāma*. (18) *Aitareyiṇaḥ*: those who study a specific branch of the Veda called the *Aitareya*. *Kāśyapāḥ*: those belonging to the *Kāśyapa* lineage. "The teachers of the *caraṇas*" means...

The word *caraṇa* denotes a group of persons who have attained unity through the study of a specific branch (*śākhā*) [of the Veda]. Thus, there is an example in the *Anuvāda* section regarding "the *caraṇas*," namely: "He established the Kaṭha and Kālāpa [schools]. (19) In that context, within the group, they are called *gurus*: those who, having performed the [initiatory] rites, teach the Veda. This is according to the statement: "He is a *guru* who, having performed the rites, transmits the Veda to him. (20) They are [also called] *paṅktipāvanas* ("purifiers of the row").

Their conduct was made beautiful by being adorned with a multitude of virtues enumerated in various sections on ancestral rites (*śrāddha*), such as being born into a lineage of those for whom gifts are given to Brahmins, not having fallen from the status of one to whom gifts are given to Brahmins, and never failing to bestow gifts upon Brahmins. (21) "Practitioners of the five fires" means those who venerate the fivefold set of fires consisting of the *gārhapatya*, *ānvāhāryapacana*, *āhavanīya*, *sabhya*, and *āvasathya*. "Firm in their vows" means...

The *sāvitra* and other vows (*vrata*) are to be undertaken at the commencement of each Veda as prescribed in their respective *Gṛhya-sūtras*. When these are completed together with the Veda, one who has returned home (*samāvṛtta*) is called a "graduate by way of Vedic vows" (*vedavratasnātaka*). If they are not completed, but one returns home before the completion of the Veda, he is a "graduate by way of learning" (*vidyāsnātaka*). Furthermore, if one returns home when the vows are completed even though learning is not yet finished, he is called a "graduate by way of vows" (*vratasnātaka*). Those by whom these have been maintained are [referred to as such]. Regarding the term "Soma-drinkers" (*somapīthin*): they are those who have drunk the Soma. By this, the performance of the Soma sacrifice is indicated.

"Those named Śambara": those whose family name is Śambara, which indicates a particular excellence, just as names such as Māra indicate the extreme cruelty of certain princes. "Proponents of Brahman" (*brahmavādinaḥ*): those whose habit is the exposition of the nature of Brahman. By this, their dedication to the meaning of the Vedas regarding the sacrifice (*adhiyajña*) and the supreme reality (*adhidaiva* or *adhibrahma*) is stated.

[5] Those who have spoken in such a manner—namely, the *śrotriyas*, those who have studied the Vedic hymns (*chandas*)—hold in high regard the eternal (*śāśvata*), constant tradition known as the Veda, which they have heard from many sources, in many ways, and together with many others (*bhūriśruta*). Is that so because such study results in abundant gains and the humiliation of others? (XX) No, he says: "In truth... (22) *Iṣṭa* refers to sacrifices and the like; *pūrta* refers to digging tanks and the like; and *tapas* refers to righteous action (*dharmya-karma*) consisting largely of physical austerity. [5]

"One born in this family" is *āmuṣyāyaṇa*. One who is the *āmuṣyāyaṇa* of them is *tadāmuṣyāyaṇa*. "Tatrabhavataḥ" means of one who is venerable. "Sugṛhītam" means a beautiful pronunciation; he whose name is like that of Bali, Karṇa, and others—names that ward off misfortune and enemies—is so described. "Pavitram kīrtanam" means his very mention, i.e., the utterance of his name, is purifying; he is likewise so described. "Lāñchanam" means a mark. Therefore, by the name borne by his father he is Śrīkaṇṭha, but by his well-known [stage] name, Bhavabhūti. She was born in the lineage of Jatūkarṇa.

Jātūkarṇī; her son. Regarding those who designate even a married woman by the *gotra* of her maternal grandfather, for one who intends to offer the funeral cakes (*piṇḍa*), water, and so forth by that very *gotra*, there is a natural sense that the statement of Bṛhaspati—“The [other] women should perform [the rites] for their husbands, and they [should do so] for them,” etc.—is in agreement with the Vasiṣṭha statement, “Prattānām itare kurvīran tāś ca teṣām,” which establishes that women must offer the funeral cakes and water by the *gotra* of their husband. Thus, this [statement of Bṛhaspati] functions as the rule determining eligibility for the offering of funeral cakes and water.

(23) "Abounding in such qualities" means: it is enriched by qualities consisting for the most part of those applications which, by their abundance, are profound in aesthetic flavor (*rasa*). (XX) "He has bestowed": he has transmitted [them] both in meaning and in application.

In this regard, some followers of the Kaula doctrine—who seek to justify the statement, "Where indeed is such freedom from fault and unanimity ever seen in the world? even in this [tradition] which abounds in qualities of such a kind—regard the detailed analysis of the body and the explicit description of objects involving aversion toward the cushion, the mattress, the bed, and the coverlet as defects. To them, he says: "And where... (verse 24).

[6] Here, indeed, there are three kinds of people who, though possessing learning and erudition, behave like cattle and are devoid of discernment. Some, by the mere acquaintance with a single well-known path, like frogs in a well, disregard the entire surface of the three worlds; unable to tolerate even the existence of the various forms prevalent in their own place of residence, they are submerged in the great mire of egoism.

But others—who, though well-established on the path of either one or two [types of poetry], possess minds filled with the skill of proficiency acquired through hearing all objects of knowledge; who are the foremost among the connoisseurs established in the assemblies of the renowned and wise; and whose hearts blossom with bliss as they immerse themselves in the unfathomable great ocean of aesthetic flavor (*rasa*)—whom do they not delight? Yet others still, whose every worldly activity has been slackened by the contemplation of the defects of sensual experience, and whose inner selves are becoming purified as all passion flows away—[whom do they not delight?]

Unable to endure the distraction caused by the experience of the mass of supreme bliss that arises spontaneously through the expansion of self-realization, which is easily accessible via the path of sensory withdrawal (*pratyāhāra*), they do not for even a moment turn toward such objects. Regarding those who are the first, he says: "Those who... and so forth. As for those who are the first, although their knowledge has a limited object, it is stained by a difficult-to-overcome egoism and is thus merely like something unreal; therefore, they "know something"—meaning, by way of irony (*kāku*), they know nothing at all.

Alternatively, those whose minds are one-pointedly absorbed in the meditation on the Supreme Brahman—the mass of bliss and consciousness—and who treat this composition, which primarily consists of the unfolding of extraordinary sensual pleasures, with the same disregard as a blade of grass—they know something that is beyond the reach of both speech and mind. That [knowledge] is indeed appropriate for them; they are those whose feet are to be saluted. This effort is not directed toward them. For a weaver never, even for a moment, weaves a loincloth intended for great kings.

As for those who belong to the first [category], the word "what" (*kiṃ*) in the phrase "do they know or do they not know? is used in a sense of censure; no effort is made toward them. Addressing those of the middle [category], he says: "But it will arise. The meaning is that because there is a conceptualization of the manifestation and disappearance of various and manifold objects in every place and at every time, even a form that was previously unacquainted may come into being by attaining its own nature through arising at another time or in another place.

Surely, even when a sentence is split, those who follow the path of grammatical coordination do not tolerate a discrepancy in the mode of comprehension, as in the case of "the owner of cows [is] with respect to horses. How much less so, then, in the case of a single [sentence]? And here, having first indicated himself in the plural with "not," he finally indicates [himself] in the singular with "mine. What kind of delusion is this, occurring even on the royal highway? Do not say so.

If, in this case, the singular and plural numbers had been intended to convey the two meanings characterized as plurality and singularity as defined by the two sūtras composed by Pāṇini, then this poet would have incurred the fault of "violation of uniformity" (*prakramabhaṅga*) and other such defects.

But when, by the rule *asmado dvayoś ca*—which contains the particle *ca* for the purpose of drawing back the word "in the singular" (*ekasmin*) from the preceding rule *jātyākhyāyām ekasmin bahuvacanam anyatarasyām*—the fact that this plural form has the same meaning as the singular is established, then how could there be any reversal? Thus, the confusion of the one who is prone to objection arises only from failing to perceive this cleverness. (25) [6]

Is it not true that he alone is authorized to compose a work for this assembly who, without any prior material, brings forth a new object and renders the world—though as solid as stone—fluid through the abundance of his own aesthetic essence? And such a person, having attained mastery over the entire range of knowable objects through intense application to the study of many scriptures—a study made delightful by ever-new lines of creative expression—is alone able to instill wonder in the heart of a connoisseur.

(26) Therefore, since the learned do not respect him as long as he does not first proclaim his own extensive learning (*bāhuśrutya*), [the author] says "even if" (*api ca*). And here, the phrase "where indeed this mode of expression occurs" is drawn back [from the previous context].

[7] Yoga: the Pātañjala-śāstra. For those contemporaneous with me, my description of my own form is indeed useless. But for those yet to come, to perform a self-description established in the *Mahābhārata* as a substitute for my own death—while disregarding my status as a trustworthy authority—would serve no purpose whatsoever; on the contrary, it would lead to great shame and contradiction with the unseen merit (*adṛṣṭa*).

(XX) And as for the excellence of the composition (*prabandhopapatti*), the connoisseurs—those virtuous persons who have determined its form according to the conventions of poets—will themselves perceive the poet’s merits by means of the beauty of the composition, which dispels the mud of all suspicions through its widespread practice; what need is there for further effort in this regard? With this intention, he says: "that which is maturity" (*yat prauḍhatvam*). Maturity (*prauḍhatva*) is the possession of creative intuition (*pratibhāna*); some hold that it belongs to the poet alone.

(XX) In reality, however, the specific figure of speech (*arthālaṅkāra*) denoted by the term *ojas* is *prauḍhatva* (boldness). This is because of the following statement: "The expression of a sentence regarding the meaning of a word, or the expression of a word regarding the meaning of a sentence; expansion and contraction, and the state of being intentional—this is *prauḍhi*. (27) An example of a sentence used for the meaning of a word: when one ought to say "the moon," one says, "the light arising from the eyes of Atri. (28) An example of a word used for the meaning of a sentence: when one ought to say "she is not a goddess, but a human woman," one says "she blinks."

(29) Regarding [the term] *vyāsa*, beginning with the phrase "in various ways," there follows an extensive explanation of the diversity of its modes. (30) *Samāsa* (abridgment), however, is the condensation of a narrative sequence that has already been introduced in detail, provided that such a summary is useful for the subject at hand—as in: "Having had his pain removed by the great medicinal herb brought by the son of the Wind, he once again became a master of lamentation for the women of Laṅkā through his arrows."

(31) *Sābhiprāyatvaṃ* (Intentionality): For example, in the verse: “This very youth, the son of Candragupta, now shines like the moon; by good fortune, a king has been born who is the refuge of the wise and whose efforts have achieved their purpose. As for the *vakula*, its ability to endure being crushed is indeed well known. *Saṃcāriṇī*: moving, mobile. *Vaijayantikā*: a banner. *Ujjvalā*: beautiful due to its stainlessness. *Vidagdhā*: refined, not vulgar. *Mugdhā*: fashioned with exquisite artistry. That which [belongs] to the *nepathya* (costume/attire)...

She whose maidenhood was manifested—that is, revealed—by her adornment, which is her arrangement [of ornaments]. She whose nature is of great majesty (*mahānubhāva*) means she whose inherent character is one of great power. She whose attendants are exceedingly noble (*atyudāra*) means she whose retinue is extremely refined (*atidakṣiṇa*); for it is said that the word *udāra* denotes "a generous donor" and "great," while *dakṣiṇa* denotes "refined" (*abhidheyavat*). And this refinement (*dākṣiṇya*) is actual on their part, brought about by the presence of the object of their determined affection. (58)

[21] Mādhava expresses what is established by his own direct experience with the words, "She is the presiding deity of that treasure of loveliness. *Rāmaṇīyakam* means loveliness (*ramyatā*); she is the presiding goddess over that treasure. Or, she is the abode of the collection—that is, the meeting place—of the essences of beauty. The meaning is that gracefulness (*lāvaṇya*) and the well-proportioned arrangement of limbs are seen in her alone to the highest degree. *Niyatam* means certainly (*nūnam*). *Kāraṇam* refers to the cause in its various forms, such as the inherent cause (*samavāyi-kāraṇa*), the instrumental cause (*karaṇa*), and so forth. As for the phrase "and Madana," the particle *ca* is used here for emphasis (*avadhāraṇe*).

The sense is that such a creation of exceedingly charming beauty was impossible for Brahmā (*Vedhas*), who is dull from his constant study of the *Purāṇas* and whose curiosity has been turned away from worldly objects. (21) "By her affectionate attendants" means by her loving female servants. "Longing" (*dohada*) means desire. "One of great fortune" refers to one whose birth is characterized by preeminent meritorious deeds.

[22] Among the ten states of desire (*kāmāvasthā*), by means of the phrase "accumulated over many days," he introduces the mental attachment and conceptualizations that delight the eyes; then, with the word "wasted" (*parimṛditā*), he indicates the previously mentioned states, showing the loss of sleep and physical emaciation. Emaciation is indicated by the very term "lotus-fiber" (*mṛṇālī*); the interruption of sleep is shown by the exhaustion produced by being crushed; and the withdrawal from sense objects is shown by the words "how could there be any engagement? and so forth.

[Objection: "But how did you perceive the transformation caused by the affliction of love through these [symptoms], which are not conclusive? To this he says: *kalayati* ("she imitates"). It means she mimics it. And so he will say later: "The passion for love is indicated by signs such as the paleness of the cheeks. (59) Another has also said: "O fierce one, if the flower-bowed god were to shake his bow before you, would your cheek not be submerged in the whiteness of the petals of the *piṇḍītaka* tree, filled with the pollen of the *ketaka*?"
(60) By means of its resemblance to the splendor of the stainless moon and its whiteness, he expresses an unsurpassed distinction and an excellence of brilliance.
(61) [22] *Vartiḥ* means a brush.

[23] *Saṃtatiḥ* means a succession; that itself is a great calamity; for the sake of that. By saying "having no cause," he shows the spontaneity (*ākasmikatā*) of the attachment of the mind. That which was seen at first and produced joy is "auspicious" (*śubham*), whereas that which later produces distress is "inauspicious" (*aśubham*). *Sarvaṃkaṣā* means all-destroying. [23]

[Makaranda: By saying "this mind is attached without regard for a cause," Mādhava implies that the attachment is accidental; Makaranda refutes this doubt regarding its spontaneity with the words "and affection... and so forth.

[24] "Is this partiality toward him without cause, such that there is no remedy for it? For he, being of the nature of affection (*sneha*), sews together the internal elements. Is this the refutation? (62) How might the Naiyāyika Mādhava gain conviction here according to the literal meaning? To this, he says: "He interweaves" (*vyatiṣajati*). "Interweaves" means he makes them interlaced, mutually joined. "Some internal [factor]"—what is it?

"In this regard, they say: 'In some cases, for someone, a certain affection blossoms, arising solely from karma cultivated through experience in previous births' (63). 'Some such thing' (ko 'pi): it cannot be pointed out as 'this' through direct perception; it is hidden, being well-established only within the inner self (adhyātma). (64) 'External conditions' (bahirupādhīn): external causes, including even such things as beauty and so forth. For even these are accepted as praiseworthy only for the purpose of silencing the mouths of malicious people. Of the 'sun' (pataṅgasya):"
When the lotus blooms at the rising of the sun, what cause for its existence can be established as a specific "this-ness"? It is the same here as well.

[24] [Mādhava: Anticipating that such a great exaltation could not possibly occur within himself, he explains it through the form of recognition, saying: "It is as if there were a recognition, as if one were to say, 'This is he. Upon seeing me, her attendants cast glances toward one another, lovely with the nectar of their smiles; in those cast glances, the expression of recognition of one previously seen is revealed without words.

In this context, the play of the eyebrows (*bhrūvilāsa*)—which arises from the grace of the *moṭṭāyita* gesture—is called "the contraction" (*nikuñcita*). This is because, upon seeing a beloved person, there occurs a physical movement born of the contemplation of previous experiences, permeated by love and wonder; and in that state, there may be a gentle bending of one eyebrow or both, which constitutes the "contraction. (65) By means of the cleverness of her attendants, the poet intends to convey the heroine’s extraordinary proficiency. [25]

[Mādhava: "Salīlam" (gracefully) is an adverbial modifier of the action of returning. The other [adverbial phrase] extends from "uttāla" to "valayāvalīkam. "Uttālāḥ" means formidable; those which are the rows of lotus-like hands—with them, the rows of bracelets become tremulous. The other [phrase] extends from "uttrasta" to "mukharam. "Uttrastāḥ" means agitated; those which are the kalahamsas; their "vibhrameṇa" means by their playful grace, that which is the charming movement of the feet.

By that tinkling of the charming, sweet-sounding anklets (*mañjīra*); by that which is interwoven with, followed by, the indistinctly sweet jingling of the small bells of her girdle (*mekhalā-kiṅkiṇī-jhaṇatkāra*); in such a way as to be resonant with that—turning back, facing toward the heroine who is approaching from behind—this is a variety of the *hṛṣṭotsuka* (joyful-longing) type. "O Princess, O daughter of the master! By good fortune!"
Thinking that "we shall grow through Ānanda," and intending precisely that unobtrusive disclosure which implies "someone belongs to someone else," their cleverness has been suggested.
(XX) [Makaranda: *Udbheda* means manifestation. How is it that this talk of women is so full of charming and delightful continuity?

*Anubandhinī*: extending. *Itthī*: woman. [MĀDHAVA] [26] "In the meantime" (*atrāntare*) means: while her friends were showing me [to her], at that moment, the state of being the teacher (*ācāryakam*)—that is, the role of the instructor—of the God of Love (*manmatha*), who had become the object of her [desire], appeared after reaching its full manifestation. (66) "Something indescribable" (*kim api*) means: it is impossible to describe its nature as anything extraordinary; as they say: "The words of great poets regarding that [state] are exhausted, and the Five-Arrowed One [Kāma] has been conquered. (67) He expresses this very point with the words "the power of speech" (*vāgvibhava*).

Sweat, paralysis, horripilation, change of voice, trembling, change of complexion, tears, and fainting—these eight are known as the *sāttvika* [emotions]. (68) Among these, because [the presence of] change of voice, change of complexion, and horripilation was impossible at that time due to being struck down by [the hero's] self-assurance, the word "abundantly" (*bhūri*) was used. Vijayi: one whose nature is victory through the destruction of the pride of independence in maintaining the state of mind instilled by the conceit of noble birth and so forth. (XX) [26]

[27] Regarding the phrase "of those that are steady and opened": that which is a sudden glance is called *ālokita* (looking); of these, "steady" means very slowly, while "opened" refers to the action of the eyelids being spread wide, as it is characterized by the statement: "But *prasṛta* is spreading. (69–70) This is a gradual spreading resulting from the desire for a full gaze, occurring first by the eyes of the hero slowly ascending toward the armpits.

(XX) "Of those with trembling creeper-like brows" refers to the *catura* (clever) movement of the brows, which is connected to the erotic sentiment (*śṛṅgāra-rasa*). Its definition is: "The *catura* [movement] consists of the brows being slightly raised and having a smooth, elongated appearance. (71) "Of those that are smooth and bud-like, and possessing expansion at the edges" refers to the gaze connected to the marvelous sentiment (*adbhuta-rasa*). As they say: "With the tips of the eyelashes contracted and the pupils raised by wonder, the gaze that is very wide and gentle is called 'marvelous' (*adbhuta*)."

(72) "The glance directed toward me" means the thought, "This is mine"; therein, by the phrase "slightly contracted," the state (*bhāva*) called *avahittha*—consisting of the concealment of a form that ought to be hidden—is expressed; this state arises from shame and is performed through a feigned display of composure that alters the manner of looking. (73) "In various ways" means manifoldly; the sense is "as objects of service. (74) By this, the intensity of longing for a sight [of her] is indicated.

Here, by the gradual expansion of the range of her gaze, there is a desire to see him further and further; by the radiance of her brow, there is the attainment of supreme bliss born of seeing him; by the gentle closing [of her eyes], there is the fulfillment of the abundance of satisfaction born of the bliss of seeing him; and by the expansion at the corners, there is the culmination in side-long glances (*kaṭākṣa*). For this very reason, he will say later: "And with those side-long glances."

And here, the *kaṭākṣa* (side-glance) consists of a sidelong look, its form being the pupil moving toward the vicinity of the ear; for this is intended by the subsequent description of the "sidelong look" in the verse beginning with *Yāntyā muhuḥ*. The *kaṭākṣa* is well known as that which severs the knot of composure residing in the heart, creates doubt regarding the existence of the beloved's passion, and is the cause of an inability to endure any state of physical or mental unease. As they say: "Suddenly, by the ears, the sharp side-glances—like swarms of bees—draw away the foremost petals of the *ketaka* flower, possessing a luster like a mountain valley. (75) [27]

[28] He says "alasavalita" and so forth, meaning: "My heart has been stolen away by those glances of yours that have turned into side-long looks. Indeed, there are ten stages of love (*kāma-avasthā*). They are as follows: "First, the delight of the eyes; then, attachment of the mind; then, longing; loss of sleep; emaciation; withdrawal from sense objects; loss of shame; madness; fainting; and death—these indeed are the ten stages of the god of love."

(76) At the moment of their first encounter with Mādhava, because the ten stages beginning with the loss of sleep—produced by long-accumulated separation—and ending with emaciation, shame, destruction of modesty, madness, and fainting, were impossible [in that instant], he describes the delight of the eyes, the attachment of the mind, the formation of mental constructs, and the withdrawal from external objects. Among these, the "delight of the eyes" is expressed by the phrase "the heart has been stolen," since this is well-known as a cause of visual pleasure even for anyone else due to its captivating nature.

"Cast away" (*apaviddha*) refers to the attachment of the mind, because it is well known that attachment has been cast away in its entirety. "Drunk" (*pīta*) means they have been brought under their own control by those [passions], because drinking consists in bringing something under one's own power through internalizing it, and because even a conceptual resolve takes the form of the conceit of establishing one's own life and self in dependence upon the favor of that [resolve].

(XX) "Uprooted" (*unmūlita*) refers to the cessation of the objects of perception; he will explain this later with the words, "There is no manifestation of discernment even regarding an object standing before one," and so forth. For when the mind is established in its own natural state, cognitions arise; but when that state is uprooted, what talk can there be of them? (77) "Without refuge" (*aśaraṇa*) indicates the absence of anyone to prevent the sudden onset of mental distraction and the like. By this also, the faultless beauty of the heroine is shown through the concealment of her defects.

And here, [in this context], the *kāntā* (lovely) glance belongs to the erotic sentiment (*śṛṅgāra-rasa*), while the *snigdhā* (affectionate) glance belongs to its corresponding mental state (*bhāva*) called *rati* (love). The definition of the *kāntā* glance is as follows: "The *kāntā* glance, arising from serenity and joy, directed toward the corners of the eyes with desire, is employed in the erotic sentiment known as *saṃbhoga* (enjoyment). (78) She displays this very glance with a languid turn. For the gaze directed toward the corners of the eyes indeed turns; and that very turning is "languid" (*alasa*) because of the presence of desire—that is, due to the absence of any interruption in the wish to look. (79)

The definition of the affectionate (*snigdha*) gaze is as follows: "The affectionate gaze, born of the emotion known as love (*rati*), is joyful, full of longing, sweet with an internal radiance, and has pupils that are slightly smiling. (80) In this context, he speaks of sweetness through the quality of innocence (*mugdhatā*). For innocence is the absence of proficiency in the practice of bold gestures; by means of that, there is sweetness, which is a state of being delicious. Through its affectionate nature, it possesses longing, because only that which is desirable becomes the object of affection.

Through "immobility," which consists in being averse to contraction, and through "slowness," which consists in resting upon a single focal point, there is a state of joy; for the object itself—the vision of the cavern that is the mass of bliss—attains the status of being the object of such a gaze. (XX) For immobility alone exists even in the innate and indeterminate state of self-awareness of the gaze; therefore, the word "slow" (*manda*) has been employed.

(81) Since even mere languor does not illuminate the specific excellence of the developed meaning (*arthaparipoṣaviśeṣa*), he has employed the word "motionless" (*niṣpanda*) as well. (XX) That which blossoms further within—that is, inside—and also wonder; in that [state], those whose pupils (*tārā*) are smiling. By this, it is said that the pupils are smiling while blossoming within. By the word "wonder" (*vismaya*), he indicates the non-abandonment of the abundant rasa of the marvelous (*adbhuta*), because it overcomes the previously introduced rasa of love (*śṛṅgāra*).

(82) And thus it is carried away by those who are agitated. Furthermore, even a thief or the like who steals something turns back, moving with very slow steps. "Turning" (*valana*) is the performance of a movement contrary to the movement that was previously undertaken; as in the phrase "the natural circle has turned," which refers to the reversal of the form previously undertaken, or as he will say later: "with his neck turned."

"Surely other insentient things may be carried away; but how can the sentient heart, while being carried off, not turn back of its own accord? This objection has already been answered: *apaviddha* is synonymous with *viddha*, *kṣipta*, and *īrita*. (83) Thus, *apaviddha* means cast aside, rejected, or, in short, defeated. And the defeat of the mind is its failure to maintain self-mastery for even a single moment.

And so, when questioned regarding the cause of his weakness and such, someone might say: "Because of the prospect of some misfortune currently befalling a certain object dear to me, there is a state of mental distraction (*cittāpakṣepa*). Now, if one examines the term *apakṣepa* according to the rules of grammar, it does not signify anything [specific]. Therefore, we consider that the word *apakṣepa* itself has simply acquired such conventional usage.

By what kind of fitness was their heart thus cast aside? Therefore, it should be understood in sequence as "bewilderingly lovely" (*mugdha*) and "affectionate" (*snigdha*). "Bewilderingly lovely" means possessing an innate, enchanting beauty; "affectionate" means characterized by specific gestures that manifest an emerging affection directed toward me. The sense is this: whose mind—even that of a sage—would not be brought under control by a glance distinguished by this pair of attributes?

One might ask: "Did you perhaps forget those means for warding off mental distraction, such as contemplating the defects of objects that are contrary to meditation on Him? To this he replies: "It was drunk"—meaning it was made free from any possibility of contact with other objects. By what capacity? To this he says: "With motionless and languid [eyes]. "Motionless" means averted from blinking and resting solely upon Me as their sole object.

The meaning is this: when her mind is offered toward me, who am thus endowed with this pair of qualifications, what need is there to mention the uprooting of the latent impressions (*saṃskāra*) regarding the defects of sense-objects for a mind that has been captivated and brought under control? And this very state is designated as "volitional construction" (*saṃkalpa*). For the perception of defects in what has not been seen is rendered completely impossible by the overwhelming excellence of her extraordinary beauty.

However, the contemplation of the faults observed by following the life stories of Rāvaṇa, Kīcaka, Nahuṣa, and others has become insubstantial, because it was countered by the realization of the intention to surrender their hearts, which was inferred from the specific gestures and glances of the heroines. Thus, first of all, I myself am incapable of restraining my mind; nor, O friend, is there any occasion here for your words of instruction. This statement, intended to seal the door of refusal, has been uprooted.

"How indeed has your love ascended to such a state?"—to this he replies: "with pupils smiling with wonder expanding within. For those who have mastered the science of the God of Love declare that this is the characteristic of a heart overflowing with the latent impressions (*vāsanā*) of sexual union. And thus, the commencement of our enjoyment has occurred.

Consequently, how could the inquiry into the commencement and fulfillment of the *saṃbhoga*—which is the source of the ultimate pinnacle of all worldly happiness, as flickering as a water-bubble at the end of a chapter that can only be compared to the bliss of the state of realizing the supreme reality—not give rise to great agitation in the mind? Enough of this excessive detail.
You should understand this commentary, which produces wonder in the multitude of refined connoisseurs, through the path of Bharata, being free from envy. [28]

He explains that faultless quality residing in the heroine, which was indicated by the phrase "having no refuge," with the words "in every respect. For if it were somehow known from any source that her mind was directed toward another man or even toward me, then, because the aesthetic flavor (*rasa*) would have been interrupted, she might remain by somehow maintaining herself; however, that has instead occurred otherwise, as he says with the word "suspected" (*saṃbhāvyamāna*).

If it is asked, "Having previously reached a certainty, how can there now be this outburst of doubt?", the answer is: "The hearts of those who fear what is undesirable are thus disposed toward prosperity"—this is nothing surprising. *Pāriplavatvam* means fickleness. "In some way or other" (*yathā kathaṃ cit*) refers to the manifestation of a poorly arranged floral design, because the mind, having been captivated by her, was sluggish in that regard. *Militāḥ* means gathered together or assembled. *Varṣavarāḥ* are those who ward off the rain (the flow of the senses); they are eunuchs (*ṣaṇḍha*); *tatprāyāḥ* means consisting mostly of them, or abundant in them.

[29] By mentioning her mounting of elephants and so forth, the heroine’s status as a woman of the highest rank is established through her birth in a great family. *Valitakandharam*: with the neck turned; *āvṛttavṛntam*: with the stalk bent. The turning of the lotus is accomplished by its revolving starting from the stalk. First it was "smeared with nectar" because it is the cause of supreme bliss; finally it was "smeared with poison" because it consists of an excess of pain. By the word "smeared" (*digdha*), which also means "embedded," the arrow-nature of the sidelong glance is suggested. By the word "deeply" (*gāḍham*), it is stated that it does not depart from the heart even for a moment. [29]

[30] Beyond delimitation (*paricchedātīta*): it is impossible for the mind to delimit it by means of its measure. "Entirety" (*sakala*) expresses the impossibility of defining it. By this, it is illustrated by the scriptural passage: "From whence words turn back, not having reached it along with the mind. (84) Furthermore, the justification for both these points is given by the phrase "in another birth. The meaning is: even if, somehow, such a transformation were to enter the path of experience, there might be the possibility of delimiting or defining it; however, that is not the case here.

"Now, having experienced both of these, one should practice them"—to this he replies with the word "viveka" (discrimination). "Gahanaḥ" means profound. "Jaḍayati" means it stupefies; "tāpayati" means it causes pain. (85) Furthermore, as for the contradiction: how can that which stupefies—that is, brings about insensibility—also cause pain? [30]

[31] Turning back at the stage of withdrawal from objects, having stated in his mind that "it transcends determination," and expanding upon this by way of its being beyond the range of all the sense organs, he says: "determination" (*pariccheda*). "Determination" refers to cognition; "manifestation" (*vyakti*) refers to the state of having a clear form. By stating that this does not exist even with respect to a proximate object, it is indicated that because the external sense organs lack the capacity to produce conceptualized cognition (*savikalpaka-vijñāna*), they do not function toward their own objects.

He says "it happens" because even the mind lacks the proficiency to engage with its own object. Previously, the power of discerning and describing the manifestation of amorous transformations never experienced before was denied; now, however, there is a distinction in that even for one who is familiar with them, the proficiency regarding the object is excluded. For this very reason, it is stated here: "even though it is practiced."

The meaning is that even regarding an object experienced many times, the recollection of it in a fragmented or partial manner brings about a sense of distaste because it does not conform to the original experience. Furthermore, the withdrawal from objects is flawed because it results in the effect of a continuous succession of afflictions in the form of torment. Torment is both physical—pertaining to external beings—and mental—pertaining to the self. And for that physical torment, the physical remedy is dependent upon the service of things such as very cool snow and the moon.

And that [state] is not possible, because we observe an extreme intensity of her torment. Furthermore, for mental torment, the contemplation (*bhāvanā*) of the object aimed at by the mind is the cause of peace; since she does not attain even a moment’s stability of mind upon a single object, what possibility can there be? Now, one might ask: "Is not incessant wandering of the mind the very nature of madness? What opportunity is there for such a state when there is withdrawal from objects? To this, he states its contrary nature with the words "what indeed" (*kim api*).
He indicates that it is something whose object is a desire even more difficult to attain, swallowed by the blow of impossibility—something indescribable.
KALAHĀSAKA: Indeed, he has been deeply struck by someone. Could it possibly be Mālatī herself?
[MAKARANDA]: Attachment: a mental affliction in the form of intense longing.

[32] "Mā mūmuhat" means: "May he not produce a derangement of the mind. The root *muha* is used in the sense of "bewilderment"; from this root, the form is derived using the *luṅ* (aorist), *ṇic* (causative suffix), *cli*, and *caṅ* (reduplication). Because of the particle *māṅ*, the addition of the augment *aṭ* is prohibited by the rule "na māṅyoge. (86) "Malīmasa" refers to a defiled transformation consisting of passion; she is "made of that" (*tanmayī*). "Jṛmbhita" means: one whose string (*guṇa*) has its tip of the fierce bow bent or coiled. [32]

[Mādhava] (Pausing): Having separated herself—that is to say, having become alone. "Nedīyasī" means nearby. She begins with words of double meaning. For the activity of a messenger proceeds once she has ascertained the hero's proficiency and intention; thus she begins. (87) [B20a] "By virtue of well-joined qualities": by means of being well-fastened threads. "Arrangement" (*saṃniveśa*): the act consisting of the arrangement of a garland of *kesara* flowers. "Novel" (*abhinava*): transcendent; "wondrous" (*vicitra*).

"Of many kinds" (*bahuprakāraḥ*): the activity (*vyāpāraḥ*) among flowers that have become objects [of art] consists in the process of arrangement (*racanānubandhaḥ*). The sense is that she, being curious to behold the skill of your craftsmanship (*nirmāṇanaipuṇam*), which delights in those various methods of stringing garlands (*mālyagrathanavikalpeṣu*), has set about it. "Fresh" (*sarasaḥ*): not withered; indeed, the very arrangement of the garland. Moreover, the "arrangement" (*saṃniveśaḥ*)—meaning the union (*saṃyogaḥ*)—between her and you is delightful due to the quality of being well-knit, that is, by virtue of the qualities being situated in mutual conformity.

It is the cause for the mutual increase of the abundance of beauty between lightning and the rain-cloud, as it were. "Eager" (*kutūhalinī*) means she is full of longing for union with you. "Novel" (*abhinava*) means unprecedented; the meaning is that she is not attached to anyone else apart from you. "Variegated" (*vicitra*) is so because it produces various transformations, or because it has attained the status of a marvel upon beholding the lotus-face of a hero such as yourself due to its appropriateness. "Of the Flower-Arrowed One" (*kusumeṣoḥ*) refers to the activity of Kāma, whose arrows are flowers.

"Let it be so that the cleverness of you two may be rendered meaningful—that is, let the loveliness of the flower’s creation and its capacity to bring about such a state be made to attain great value. [Mādhava: "By her who was questioned: by her who was asked. She is called *dhātreyikā* (the foster-sister) to indicate that she is a vessel of confidence in the secret conversations of maidens. ... Because she grew up together with her from birth, he mentioned the *dhātreyikā* first, owing to her preeminence. (88)

Kalahāṃsaka: What, do you mean Mālatī? By good fortune, the divine Lord of the Flower-Arrows has truly triumphed! If Mādhava has also fallen in love with Mālatī—whose passion was aroused by the drawing of his portrait—then indeed the God of Love has triumphed. Among common folk, the mere manifestation [of passion] receives the designation of "love" (smaratā); but here, it is designated as his "triumph" (vilasati).

[Makaranda: "Of great respect" (*bahumānasya*): of honor; "inexhaustibility" (*aparyāptiḥ*): the absence of limitation by measure. The sense is that the gravity of this task is of manifold kinds. [Mādhava: "Being pursued. (89) "By one who is intent" (*abhiniviṣṭayā*): by one who has applied herself with excessive effort. "Agitation" (*vihastatvam*): confusion. "By a tumultuous [confusion]" (*saṃkulena*): by a pervasion consisting of moving here and there.

[Makaranda: "Well-connected" means well-integrated. "Visual passion" (*cakṣūrāga*) refers to the affection felt precisely for the person who is seen. Thus, by reflecting on the heroine's own nature, it has been understood that her infatuation with love is directed toward you. He says "moreover" (*api ca*) because there is yet another sign of her prior affection for you. [33] "Intermingled" (*saṃbhinnāḥ*) means joined together.

Regarding the word *ca* in the phrase *niveditaṃ ca*, Mākaranda employed it with a specific intention toward another indicative mark (*liṅgāntara*). That which was revolving in his mind due to the intensity of his longing, Mādhava himself now expresses by saying *kiṃ ca*. (90) *Niveditam*: the act of reporting (*nivedana*). Having attained this, which constitutes the meaning of the treatise—having experienced it through the application of effort—he has reached the state of one whose nature is free from the heat [of afflictions]. 10.49cd–50ab. The *dharmāmbhas* (water of the Dharma) is the water that washes away the stains of the afflictions (*kleśa*). It is called "water" because it is like water in its capacity to cleanse. This is the "water of the Dharma," and it is "attained" (*prāpta*) by him. That is to say, he has obtained it. Furthermore, it is "vigama" (departed); that is, it has vanished. What has vanished? The aforementioned "heat" (*gharma*), which consists of the afflictions. That is to say, he has become one who is free from the heat of the afflictions. 10.50cd–51ab. Moreover, having attained this, he has reached the stage of a "stream-enterer" (*srotaāpanna*). How so? Because he has entered the stream of the noble Dharma. The "stream" is the path of the noble ones; it is called a "stream" because it flows toward *nirvāṇa*. He has entered that stream; therefore, he is a "stream-enterer. Furthermore, he has "crossed over the ocean of existence" (*bhavārṇava*). The "ocean" is the great ocean of cyclic existence (*saṃsāra*). He has crossed over that; therefore, he is one who has "crossed over the ocean of existence. 10.51cd–52ab. Moreover, he has "reached the shore of the city of peace" (*śāntipura*). The "city" is the city of *nirvāṇa*. The "shore" is the boundary of that city. He has reached that shore; therefore, he is one who has "reached the shore of the city of peace. 10.52cd–53ab. Furthermore, he has "attained the supreme fruit of the holy life" (*brahmacaryaphala*). The "fruit of the holy life" is the fruit of the religious life (*brahmacarya*). It is "supreme" because it is unsurpassed. He has attained that; therefore, he is one who has "attained the supreme fruit of the holy life. 10.53cd–54ab. Moreover, he has "become one who has reached the end of suffering" (*kṛtānta-duḥkha*). "End" (*anta*) means cessation. "Reached the end" (*kṛtānta*) means one who has brought [suffering] to its conclusion. "Suffering" (*duḥkha*) refers to the various forms of suffering such as birth, aging, sickness, and death. He has become one who has reached the end of that; therefore, he is one who has "become one who has reached the end of suffering. 10.54cd–55ab. Furthermore, he has "become one who has transcended all fear" (*sarvabhayātīta*). "Fear" (*bhaya*) refers to the various fears such as the fear of kings, thieves, fire, water, and enemies. He has transcended all of them; therefore, he is one who has "become one who has transcended all fear. 10.55cd–56ab. Moreover, he has "become one who has attained the state of being free from all calamities" (*sarvopadravavigata*). "Calamity" (*upadrava*) refers to the various misfortunes such as hunger, thirst, cold, heat, wind, rain, and illness. He has become one who is free from all of them; therefore, he is one who has "become one who has attained the state of being free from all calamities. 10.56cd–57ab. Furthermore, he has "become one who has reached the state of being free from all defilements" (*sarvamalāpagata*). "Defilement" (*mala*) refers to the various impurities such as greed, hatred, and delusion. He has become one who is free from all of them; therefore, he is one who has "become one who has reached the state of being free from all defilements. 10.57cd–58ab.
